reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ESC & ACC-AHA guidelines
clinicalPearls: PAD is atherosclerotic narrowing of the arteries supplying the limbs, most often the lower extremities, and is a marker of widespread atherosclerosis with high cardiovascular risk
The classic symptom is intermittent claudication, exertional muscle pain in the calf, thigh, or buttock that is relieved by rest, though many patients are asymptomatic or have atypical leg symptoms
Examination may reveal diminished or absent pulses, arterial bruits, cool skin, hair loss, and delayed capillary refill

The ankle-brachial index is a simple, key bedside test; a reduced value confirms obstruction, while an abnormally high or incompressible value suggests medial calcification, common in diabetes and chronic kidney disease
Critical limb ischaemia, with rest pain, non-healing ulcers, or gangrene, indicates severe disease that threatens the limb and warrants urgent vascular assessment
Acute limb ischaemia is a vascular emergency presenting with the classic features of a suddenly painful, pale, pulseless, cold limb with sensory and motor changes
Management emphasises aggressive cardiovascular risk reduction, structured exercise, and antiplatelet and statin therapy, with revascularisation for lifestyle-limiting or limb-threatening disease
Because PAD reflects systemic atherosclerosis, coexisting coronary and cerebrovascular disease should be actively addressed
reference.pathophysiology: PAD is usually caused by atherosclerosis, in which lipid-laden plaque progressively narrows the arterial lumen and limits blood flow to the limbs. When demand rises with exertion, a flow-limiting stenosis cannot meet the increased oxygen requirement of exercising muscle, producing the ischaemic pain of claudication. As disease advances, resting perfusion becomes inadequate, causing rest pain, impaired wound healing, ulceration, and tissue loss (critical limb ischaemia). Acute limb ischaemia results from sudden occlusion by thrombosis of a diseased segment or by embolism, abruptly interrupting flow and threatening tissue viability within hours.
additionalDifferentials: Lumbar spinal stenosis causing neurogenic claudication
Deep vein thrombosis and chronic venous insufficiency
additionalInvestigations: Ankle-brachial index measurement, with exercise testing if resting values are equivocal
Duplex ultrasound to localise and grade stenoses
CT or MR angiography, or invasive angiography, to plan revascularisation
Assessment of cardiovascular risk factors including lipids, glucose, and smoking status
Toe-brachial index or other measures when arteries are incompressible
Wound and infection assessment in patients with ulcers or tissue loss
redFlags: MEDICAL EMERGENCY: acute limb ischaemia with a painful, pale, pulseless, cold limb and sensory or motor deficit requiring urgent revascularisation
Critical limb ischaemia with rest pain, non-healing ulceration, or gangrene threatening the limb
Rapidly progressive tissue loss or signs of spreading infection in an ischaemic foot
Sudden onset of severe leg symptoms suggesting embolic occlusion
reference.prognosis: Limb prognosis is often stable in claudication with good risk-factor control, but PAD signals a substantially elevated risk of myocardial infarction, stroke, and cardiovascular death; critical and acute limb ischaemia carry high risks of amputation and mortality without timely intervention.
pitfalls: Relying on a normal or high ankle-brachial index in patients with incompressible calcified vessels, as in diabetes or renal disease
Attributing exertional leg pain to musculoskeletal or neurogenic causes and missing PAD
Focusing on the limb while neglecting the high coronary and cerebrovascular risk
Failing to recognise acute limb ischaemia as an emergency requiring urgent revascularisation
management: Provide cardiovascular risk reduction as the foundation with statin therapy, antiplatelet therapy and control of blood pressure and glucose, since PAD marks widespread atherosclerosis
Support smoking cessation as the single most important modifiable measure
Prescribe a supervised walking exercise programme to improve claudication distance
Offer cilostazol for symptomatic claudication where not contraindicated

Revascularise by endovascular angioplasty or stenting, or surgical bypass, for lifestyle-limiting claudication refractory to conservative care and urgently for critical limb ischaemia with rest pain, non-healing ulcers or gangrene
Treat acute limb ischaemia as a vascular emergency with anticoagulation and urgent embolectomy, thrombolysis or revascularisation to salvage the limb
Provide meticulous foot care, wound management and treatment of infection in tissue loss, and refer to vascular surgery
